Parametric-bootstrap p-values for a specification test

Source: R/tests_fit.R
boot_pvalue.Rd

Calibrates any test in the package (or a user function returning a data frame with a statistic column) by the parametric bootstrap: B outcome vectors are drawn from the fitted model with the covariates held fixed, the model is refit on each (with the fit's own covariance type; a bootstrap covariance is replaced by the analytic one inside the replicates), the test is recomputed, and the p-value of every row is \((1 + k) / (B' + 1)\), with \(B'\) the replicates that succeeded and \(k\) the number of their statistics at least as large as the observed one. This is the reference distribution that remains valid when the asymptotic chi-square is unreliable (small samples, rare alternatives, Hausman statistics with a non-positive-definite covariance difference).

Usage

boot_pvalue(object, test, B = 199L, cores = 1L, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted mnl() model.

test

A test function taking the fitted mnl() model as its first argument, whose null hypothesis is that model, and returning a data frame with a statistic column (e.g. hausman_mcfadden(), small_hsiao(), fp_tests(), nested_lm_test(), captivity_test(); not hl_test(), which returns a list, and not term_test() or combine_test(), whose null is a restriction of the model).

B

Number of bootstrap replicates (default 199).

cores

Number of parallel workers.

...

Further arguments to test.

Value

The test's data frame with the column p.boot added (and p.value kept), the attribute "boot_statistics" holding the \(B\) replicate statistics per row, "B", "n_failed" (replicates whose refit or test failed, dropped), "n_flagged" (replicates whose refit raised a warning; they are kept, and the count is printed with the method line), "flagged" (which replicates, aligned with the columns of "boot_statistics"), "flag_reasons" (a table of the first warning of each flagged refit), and, when some but not all replicates are flagged, "p.boot_unflagged", the bootstrap p-values over the unflagged replicates. When the observed fit raised no such warning, those are the replicates that resemble the data: a separated simulated sample can produce an extreme statistic that says nothing about the data at hand.

Details

Frequency weights (integers) are expanded to one row per case, for the simulated data and for the observed statistic alike, so that both follow one definition; a test that refits from the data rather than from the fitted design cannot be calibrated with weights (the package's own tests all work from the fitted design; a user-written test that refits with mnl() from object$data is one that refits from the data), and a test that calls update() on the fit re-evaluates the original call on the original data, so it must work from the fitted object (its data component carries the simulated response). Replicates whose refit warns (a separated simulated sample, an ill-conditioned information matrix) are kept and counted (n_flagged): a few are expected with rare alternatives; when they are many, the statistic itself is unstable on data like these, and the p-value should be read with that in mind. The attribute p.boot_unflagged leaves the flagged replicates out. It is a p-value conditional on unflagged samples, whose size has not been studied, and is no substitute for p.boot. A replicate in which an alternative is never chosen, and whose maximum-likelihood estimate therefore does not exist, is dropped and counted in n_failed, so the bootstrap distribution is conditional on the estimate existing. For mnl() without fixed effects, separation() decides that (an alternative without a constant can be never chosen and still have an estimate); for the other models an alternative with coefficients of its own must be chosen (boot_lr_test() keeps such replicates where the separation check applies). For a penalized fit, whose estimates exist without every alternative chosen, such replicates are kept and refit under the same penalty.

The replicates are drawn from the fitted model, so the test's null hypothesis must be that model: the IIA tests, nested_lm_test(), captivity_test(), and user-written tests of that kind. term_test() and combine_test() test a restriction of the fitted model, which the replicates would not satisfy, and are refused; for a term, fit the model without it and use boot_lr_test(). The package's tests derived for maximum-likelihood estimates refuse a penalized fit (firth = TRUE or a prior), so they cannot be calibrated on one here.

Every replicate's outcomes are drawn in the session before any refit runs, so a result under set.seed() does not depend on cores (for a test with random draws of its own, such as small_hsiao(), when its seed is fixed). The replicates draw cases independently: with clustered data the bootstrap distribution ignores the clustering.

See also

hausman_mcfadden(), small_hsiao(), fp_tests(), nested_lm_test()

Other IIA tests: fp_tests(), hausman_mcfadden(), iia_tests(), nested_lm_test(), small_hsiao()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(3)
d <- rmnl(800, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5), d = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.9)))
m <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)
boot_pvalue(m, hausman_mcfadden, B = 99, drop = "b")
#> Hausman-McFadden test of IIA (variance difference) -- parametric bootstrap, 99 replicates 
#>  alternative statistic df p.value   psd n_restricted p.boot
#>            b     1.537  6   0.957 FALSE          483   0.39
#> Note: psd = FALSE: the covariance difference is not positive semi-definite. A negative statistic is no evidence against IIA (p-value 1); a positive one is unreliable (the difference form over-rejects); use vcov = "joint". 
# }
